summary: PRISMA is an interactive geospatial tool that leverages NASA POWER satellite data to visualize historical UV radiation anomalies across Colombian cities. While the Ministry of Environment monitors precursor gases (like NO₂) through ground stations, they lack a continuous spatial map of UV radiation—the "engine" that catalyzes these gases into toxic smog and acid rain. Using a Z-score statistical approach (±1.5σ), our tool transforms raw NASA data into an accessible map where red, blue, and gray dots indicate significant positive, negative, or normal UV anomalies for each year. This addresses the challenge of identifying where and when environmental changes are statistically significant. By providing the missing climate layer for the Ministry's annual reports, PRISMA enables authorities to calculate a per-city Photochemical Risk Index, empowering data-driven public health decisions without the need for costly physical infrastructure.
details:
PRISMA is an interactive web platform that visualizes historical UV radiation anomalies across Colombian cities using satellite data from NASA POWER (ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX). The tool processes over 20 years of data (2001–2024), calculates the historical average and standard deviation for each city, and uses a Z-score methodology to classify each year as "Normal," "Anomalously High" (red), or "Anomalously Low" (blue) based on a ±1.5σ threshold. Users can select any year from a dropdown menu, and the map instantly updates, showing colored dots where the size reflects the magnitude of the anomaly.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
The primary beneficiary is the Ministry of Environment and regional environmental authorities. While they currently monitor precursor gases (like NO₂) through ground stations, they lack a continuous spatial map of UV radiation—the "engine" that catalyzes these gases into toxic smog and acid rain. PRISMA fills this gap by providing the missing climate layer for their annual air quality reports. This allows authorities to calculate a per-city Photochemical Risk Index, identifying where and when local pollutants are most likely to become dangerous. The impact is direct: improved public health policies and targeted environmental interventions without the need for costly physical infrastructure.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Programming Language: Python (for data processing and statistical analysis), Java Script.
  • Libraries: pandas and numpy (data manipulation), scipy.stats (linear regression, Kendall tau, Theil-Sen). For Java Script we used, Cesium JS, React, Vite.
  • Data Source: NASA POWER API (satellite-derived UV index data).
  • Frontend: Leaflet.js (interactive web mapping), HTML/CSS/JavaScript.
  • Visualization: Cesium.
